podcast.title: Nervous Breakdown and HIV/AIDS Anxiety (Leading up to 1985-1987)
podcast.body: Michael Stipe suffered a "complete nervous breakdown" leading up to 1985, which his bandmates misconstrued as him being "impossible." During this period, he was consumed by terror, believing his past behaviors as a gay man would lead to his death from AIDS/HIV. This paranoia manifested as dread with every cold until he underwent an anonymous HIV test in 1987. This emotional turmoil significantly impacted the recording of R.E.M.'s third album, "Fables of the Reconstruction," contributing to it being the band's least favorite and a commercial disappointment. "Until it was finally able to get an anonymous HIV test in 1987, there was a sense of dread and paranoia every time I got a cold."

podcast.title: Guarded Sexuality and Self-Identification (2011 Revelations)
podcast.body: For many years, Michael Stipe maintained strict privacy regarding his sexuality, leading to public assumptions that he might be gay. However, he later identified himself as "an equal opportunity letch," clarifying that he was not exclusively straight, gay, or bisexual. In December 2011, revelations to the New York Times explained that his early career reputation for being grumpy, aloof, and distant stemmed from being "terrified out of his mind" due to fears of contracting HIV/AIDS as a gay man. "He would later identify, and this is a quote, an equal opportunity letch and not someone who was straight gay or bisexual."

podcast.title: Discovery of Patti Smith
podcast.body: At the age of 15, while in detention, Michael Stipe discovered Patti Smith and the CBGB punk scene by reading an article in *Cream* magazine. He was so captivated by a picture of Patti Smith that he immediately bought a copy of *Horses* on its release day and became "hooked." "15-year-old Michael Steip discovered Patty Smith and others who played at CBGB when he was in detention Someone left a copy of cream magazine under the desk and he read an article about CBGB and the punk scene there And then he saw a picture of Patty in it and he went and bought it A copy of horses the day that it came out and he was hooked."

xref.title: Michael Stipe's Nervous Breakdown and HIV/AIDS Fears (Leading up to 1985)
xref.body: Michael Stipe experienced a "complete nervous breakdown" leading up to 1985, which went unrecognized by his bandmates, who perceived him as being "impossible." This period was marked by intense fear as a gay man, terrified that his past behaviors would lead to death from AIDS/HIV, a condition not widely discussed at the time. This dread and paranoia, especially during common colds, persisted until he received an anonymous HIV test in 1987. His mental state during this time, coupled with the cold, damp recording conditions in London, notably affected the sound and commercial performance of R.E.M.'s third album, "Fables of the Reconstruction." "Most of the time that I was a pop star, I loved it, but in this period leading up to 1985, I had this complete nervous breakdown and nobody recognized it."

xref.title: Major Label Signing (1988)
xref.body: By 1987, R.E.M. felt they had exhausted their potential as an indie band and faced a choice between a career stall or signing with a major label. They signed with Warner Brothers on April 8, 1988, receiving a $6 million check. Michael Stipe stated the move was necessary for "worldwide" distribution, as IRS's distribution capabilities had reached their limit. Peter Buck reflected on the band's ongoing struggle to balance artistic integrity with commercial moves, acknowledging they were "part of the machine." "So it came to pass on April 8, 1988, R.E.M. signed with Warner Brothers and took home a $6 million check."

xref.title: Origin of Band Name (2019 Biography)
xref.body: Contrary to the long-standing rumor that R.E.M. chose their name randomly from a dictionary, a 2019 biography asserts that the band's name was derived from the initials of Robert Eugene Miteyard, an obscure photographer from Kentucky. Michael Stipe was reportedly a fan of Miteyard, who signed his prints as REM. "But according to a 2019 biography, REM was actually taken from the initials for Robert Eugene Miteyard, an obscure photographer from Kentucky who signed his prints as REM."

xref.title: Balancing Art and Commerce
xref.body: Peter Buck articulated the band's struggle to balance artistic integrity with commercial interests, expressing their fear of diluting the band's essence while acknowledging their role within the music industry "machine." Michael Stipe further explained the move to Warner Brothers by stating that IRS's distribution capabilities had reached their limit, necessitating a partnership with a label capable of global reach. "In our own case, R.E.M. is always trying to figure out where the line is between commerce and what we do, because it means something to us."

xref.title: Band's Love for Record Collecting
xref.body: The members of R.E.M. were avid record collectors, a passion notably influenced by guitarist Peter Buck, who used to work as a record store clerk. Michael Stipe was even one of Buck's regular customers. This love for records meant the band often took opportunities to go record shopping while on the road. "Now the guys in REM were all fans of collecting records after all guitarist Peter Buck used to be a record store clerk And one of his big customers was Michael Steip"

xref.body: Michael Stipe of R.E.M. co-founded C100, one of his two movie production companies, which specializes in alternative film. This venture allows him to engage with the film industry outside of traditional Hollywood structures. "He has two movie production companies. There's C100, which is into alternative film."

xref.title: Career Trajectory and Influences
xref.body: Originally from Nebraska, Matthew Sweet relocated to Athens, Georgia, where he was involved in a band with Michael Stipe's sister. His career took some time to gain momentum, but it found its footing with his third album, "Girlfriend," in 1991. He exemplified the "Beatlesque" approach of 90s alt-rock, paying close attention to pre-Sgt. Pepper influences. "Matthew Sweet, a dude originally from Nebraska who ended up in Athens, Georgia in a band with Michael Steibes' sister."

xref.body: Following Arthur Kane's death, the remaining two Dolls, David Johansen and Sylvain Sylvain, decided to continue as a duo, recording a "pretty good record" titled "One Day, it will please us to remember even this," which included guest appearances by Iggy Pop and Michael Stipe. "This left us with just two dolls. David Johansson and Sylvain Sylvain. They decided to carry on and record an album."

xref.title: Formation Anecdote
xref.body: R.E.M.'s origins began when record store clerk Peter Buck initiated a conversation with art student Michael Stipe, who was often seeking out unusual 12-inch singles. Inspired by the success of friends like The B-52s, Peter and Michael later connected with Mike Mills and Bill Berry, two musicians from Macon, Georgia, to form the band. "a record store clerk named Peter Buck struck up a conversation with an art student who was always looking for strange 12-inch singles, and his name was Michael Steip."

xref.title: Formation and First Gig
xref.body: Guitarist Peter Buck, a record store clerk, struck up a conversation with art student Michael Stipe, who was often looking for strange 12-inch singles. Encouraged by the success of their friends, The B-52s, Peter and Michael recruited bassist Mike Mills and drummer Bill Berry, both from Macon, Georgia. Their first gig was at a friend's birthday party in a deconsecrated church in Athens on April 5th, 1980. "Shortly after the B-52s began to attract attention, a record store clerk named Peter Buck struck up a conversation with an art student who was always looking for strange 12-inch singles. His name was Michael Steip, encouraged by the success of their friends, the B-52s."

xref.title: Michael Stipe's Dislike for "Superman"
xref.body: Michael Stipe found the song "Superman" to be "boring" and refused to sing lead on it. He was outvoted by the rest of the band, leading to Mike Mills taking over lead vocal duties for the track, with Stipe providing backup vocals. "Everybody in the band really liked it except Michael Steip Boring he said But Steip was outvoted and the song was recorded for the band's 1986 album Life's Rich Pageant"

xref.title: Origin of "Superman"
xref.body: Bass player Mike Mills discovered the original "Superman" on the B-side of a 1969 seven-inch single by a forgotten Texas band called Clique while browsing in a flea market. The band liked the B-side enough to record it for *Life's Rich Pageant*, despite Michael Stipe disliking it. "This is how a bass player Mike Mills ended up in a flea market looking at old singles And he found a seven-inch single released in 1969 by a long forgotten Texas band called clique"

xref.title: R.E.M. Tour Support
xref.body: "The Bends" initially flopped but gained traction after Michael Stipe of R.E.M. took Radiohead "under REM's wing," offering them support slots on their tour. This provided crucial exposure and advice from R.E.M. The two bands "got along famously" and engaged in pranks, such as Michael Stipe sending a radio-controlled car onto the stage during Radiohead's set. "It never really caught on until Michael Steip took Radiohead under REM's wing and offered them support slots on their monster tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Single Cell Pictures – Hollywood-Style Film Production Company
xref.body: Michael Stipe also co-founded Single Cell Pictures, his second movie production company, which focuses on Hollywood-style films. Through this company, he has served as executive producer for notable movies such as *Being John Malkovich*, *Man on the Moon*, and *Velvet Goldmine*. "And then there's single cell pictures, which is all about Hollywood style films."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Speculation on Undied Life
xref.body: If Kurt had not died, it is speculated that he would have separated from Nirvana for a solo project with different musicians, possibly Buzz Osborne of the Melvins and Michael Stipe of R.E.M., with whom he had discussed working. This solo record would likely have had a more acoustic feel with string arrangements. "Well my guess would be that he would have separated himself from Nirvana for his next project using different musicians. Maybe people like, I don't know, Buzz A's, One of the Melvin's and most likely Michael Stipe of R.E.M."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Support for Radiohead
xref.body: Michael Stipe of R.E.M. took Radiohead "under REM's wing" and offered them support slots on their tour, which was a "huge, huge help" for Radiohead's exposure and provided them with advice. The bands "got along famously" and exchanged pranks on tour, such as Michael Stipe sending a radio-controlled car onto the stage during Radiohead's set. "It never really caught on until Michael Steip took Radiohead under REM's wing and offered them support slots on their monster tour."
